cases.abstract: Imitation policies trained on a small set of wrist-camera demonstrations can fail when execution drifts beyond the observed trajectories. DMD expands training coverage by synthesizing nearby camera views and assigning them corrective actions computed from an expert trajectory. A pretrained, pose-conditioned diffusion model is adapted using task demonstrations, task-agnostic play, or both; reconstructed camera poses supply supervision for the generated views. Labels target a later demonstration frame rather than the immediate successor, avoiding backward commands when a generated viewpoint has already passed that successor. Real-robot experiments cover pushing, stacking, pouring, and shirt hanging. With 24 pushing demonstrations, DMD succeeds in all 10 trials, compared with three for behavior cloning. In a separate cup-arrangement evaluation using 1,447 demonstrations, augmentation raises success from 4/25 to 16/25 on five unseen cups in a new environment; both policies receive identically cropped, rectified images. These results support augmenting both regression and diffusion policies with off-trajectory supervision, including beyond the low-data regime. The approach assumes recoverable perturbations and cannot undo irreversible events such as spilling beans.
cases.methods: For each demonstration, structure from motion estimates camera poses and relative transforms between image pairs. These pairs fine-tune a pretrained conditional diffusion model to synthesize a view for a requested pose displacement. Augmentation samples nearby virtual camera positions and computes the transform from each virtual pose to a later pose on the original trajectory. That transform supplies the action target, pairing an off-trajectory observation with a command intended to resume task progress rather than reusing the original image's label. Choosing the immediate successor can produce backward commands when the virtual camera has already passed it. The implementation instead targets the third subsequent frame, balancing the observed plateau in directional-error improvement against losing more terminal frames at larger offsets. Original and generated image-action pairs are then combined for policy training, assuming that the sampled states remain recoverable.
cases.results: On held-out pushing trajectories, adding DMD to color jitter and horizontal flips lowers median directional error from 0.355 to 0.328 radians. The corresponding robot comparison is much larger: success increases from 3/10 for behavior cloning to 10/10 for DMD with 24 demonstrations. Thus, a modest improvement in single-frame prediction accompanies a substantial difference over complete executions, consistent with accumulated errors being consequential. With eight demonstrations, DMD still succeeds in 8/10 trials versus 2/10 for behavior cloning, but its view generator is trained on separate play data, not those eight demonstrations alone. Benefits also persist with a larger dataset: on five unseen cups in a new lab, augmentation improves a retrained Diffusion Policy from 4/25 to 16/25 successes using matched starts and the same cropped, rectified inputs. Failures remain in this shifted setting, and the recovery labels rely on reversible deviations; once manipulation spills the contents of a cup, returning the camera to an expert pose cannot restore the task state.
cases.notes: Prioritized corrective supervision over image-generation architecture. The eight-demonstration setting uses a diffusion model trained on play data. Cup-arrangement comparisons use retrained policies with cropped, rectified images, not the original fisheye-input UMI baseline. Pouring results are omitted because the task-only and task-plus-play comparisons were separate randomized A/B tests with different BC outcomes. Reported percentages are descriptive trial outcomes, not population guarantees.

cases.abstract: Fine bimanual manipulation requires both demonstrations that capture delicate coordination and policies that avoid accumulating errors during long, high-frequency executions. ALOHA provides an open-source teleoperation platform assembled within a $20,000 budget, using joint-space coupling between smaller leader arms and larger follower arms, modified grippers, and four RGB cameras. Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) learns from these demonstrations by predicting sequences of joint targets rather than isolated actions. Overlapping predictions are combined for each execution time, retaining frequent feedback while smoothing transitions; conditional variational training accommodates variation in human demonstrations. The main evaluation spans two simulated and six physical tasks, with 50 demonstrations per physical task except threading, which uses 100. Across 25 trials per physical task and one training seed, ACT achieves 88% success on opening an upright slider bag and 96% on battery insertion, while four tuned imitation baselines achieve no final successes on either task. Threading remains difficult, reaching only 20% success. A randomized six-participant study further finds that 50 Hz teleoperation reduces completion time relative to 5 Hz. Together, the platform and policy enable learning several precise behaviors without eliminating perception and hardware constraints.
cases.methods: ACT treats each observation as the start of a sequence of future joint targets for both arms. Demonstrations pair follower joint positions and four camera views with leader joint targets; using leader targets preserves the command differences through which the position controller applies contact forces. A transformer policy predicts an action chunk, reducing the effective decision horizon and representing short stretches of temporally dependent human behavior. During deployment, the policy is queried at every step rather than waiting for a whole chunk to finish. Predictions from overlapping chunks are exponentially weighted only when they refer to the same execution time, smoothing motion without averaging neighboring actions that may serve different purposes. Training uses a conditional variational autoencoder to represent variation among demonstrated action sequences, with reconstruction and Gaussian-prior regularization. At inference, its encoder is discarded and the latent variable is set to zero, yielding deterministic predictions from current observations.
cases.results: With temporal ensembling disabled, increasing ACT's chunk length from one to 100 actions raises mean simulation success from 1% to 44% across two tasks trained with either scripted or human demonstrations. Longer chunks slightly reduce success, suggesting a tradeoff between horizon reduction, responsiveness, and sequence-modeling difficulty. Conditional variational training addresses a different issue: removing it lowers success on human demonstrations from 35.3% to 2%, averaged across the two simulated tasks, while changing little for deterministic scripted data. This contrast ties its benefit to demonstration variability rather than a universal advantage of the objective. Hardware feedback also matters: in a randomized six-participant study, 50 Hz teleoperation reduces average threading time from 33 to 20 seconds and cup-separation time from 16 to 10 seconds relative to 5 Hz. These component benefits do not make fine manipulation uniformly reliable. The learned threading policy completes only 20% of trials despite 100 demonstrations, with premature grasping and missed insertion exposing remaining visual-localization difficulties.
cases.notes: Retained ALOHA and ACT as complementary contributions, separating human teleoperation evidence from autonomous policy success. Counts follow the six physical task definitions and tables; the body refers to three remaining tasks although four are listed. Temporal-ensemble comparisons were separately tuned and hurt VINN, so no general smoothing advantage is claimed. Candy unwrapping had 0/10 initial successes but succeeded on 3/5 candies when each received ten attempts; the retry protocol is not a single-attempt success rate. Hardware torque and gripper limitations remain distinct from perceptual policy failures.
